kurals.tamil:
நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா தமர்நீரும்
இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nizhalneerum innaadha innaa thamarneerum
innaavaam innaa seyin.
kurals.meaning: Shade and water are comforts, yet they become harmful when they breed sickness; in the same way, the closeness of one's own people becomes painful when they do harm.
kurals.elementary: A shady tree and a cool drink are lovely on a hot day, but if the water is dirty it can make you sick. Family and friends are meant to be like shade and water, so when someone close to us starts hurting us, it feels even worse than a stranger doing it.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a paired simile: nizhal-neer (நிழல்நீர், shade and water), the archetypal comforts of a hot land, are innaadha (இன்னாத, painful) when innaa (இன்னா, harmful, i.e. disease-bearing); so too thamar-neer (தமர்நீர், the 'nature' or disposition of one's kin) becomes innaavaam when it does harm. The wordplay on neer, meaning both 'water' and 'nature/quality', is deliberate and is reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar's and Kalaignar's glosses, which read thamar-neer as the qualities of kinsfolk. Solomon Pappaiah extends thamar to one's own party or faction, showing how modern commentators read utpakai (உட்பகை, enmity from within) politically as well as domestically. In the traditional reading framed by Parimelazhagar, the Porul section addresses a ruler, so the 'kin' include courtiers and relations around the throne. Text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Queen Kaikeyi, a member of Dasharatha's own household and once his favourite, uses two old boons to force Rama's exile, breaking the king's heart.
hinduism.explanation: The person closest to the king, whose presence should have been a comfort, becomes the source of the household's greatest grief.
hinduism.tie_back: Like shade and water turned harmful, a beloved relative turned hostile brings pain precisely because she was trusted.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A well-known narrative illustration of harm from within the family; the Kural's shade-and-water image has no direct counterpart.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist laments betrayal by an intimate who shared his table, a verse the Gospel of John later applies to Judas.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that harm from those who should sustain us, like food and shade, is uniquely bitter.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on betrayal by intimates; lacks the Kural's analogy of comforts turning harmful.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, among your wives and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive - then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that even the nearest family can, at times, work against one's good, while still urging forgiveness.
islam.tie_back: Both texts recognize that those meant to be our comfort can become a source of harm.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear thematic overlap on hostility within the household; the Qur'an adds a call to pardon that the Kural does not.

judaism.quote_or_event: Absalom, King David's own son, wins the hearts of the people at the city gate and then raises a rebellion that drives his father out of Jerusalem.
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew Bible presents the revolt as a tragedy precisely because it comes from David's own child.
judaism.tie_back: As the Kural warns, kin who turn to harm become a deeper misery than strangers.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel on harm from close kin; not a teaching statement like the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, the Buddha's own cousin and a monk in his order, plotted against the Buddha's life and tried to split the Sangha.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist tradition remembers Devadatta as the danger that arose from inside the Buddha's own family and community.
buddhism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's point that a relative who turns harmful is like refreshment that has turned to sickness.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel of kin-enmity; no direct analogue to the shade-and-water image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Deianira sends her husband Heracles a robe smeared with what she believes is a love charm from the centaur Nessus; it is poison, and it burns him to death.
greek_mythology.explanation: A gift meant to bind and comfort becomes deadly, delivered by the hero's own wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's image of comforts that turn harmful and of harm arriving through one's own household.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Deianira acts unknowingly, not from enmity, so the match is on the image of comfort turned to harm rather than on hostility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Paracelsus argued that all things can be poison and that only the dose decides whether a thing heals or harms.
philosophy.explanation: The principle holds that even beneficial substances become harmful under the wrong conditions.
philosophy.tie_back: It echoes the first half of the Kural, where shade and water, ordinarily good, become harmful.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches only the shade-and-water image, not the Kural's point about kinsfolk; a weak, next-best parallel.

kurals.tamil:
வாள்போல பகைவரை அஞ்சற்க அஞ்சுக
கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaalpola pakaivarai anjarka anjuka
kelpol pakaivar thotarpu.
kurals.meaning: Do not fear enemies who come openly like a drawn sword; fear instead the company of enemies who pose as kinsmen or friends.
kurals.elementary: A bully who shouts at you from across the playground is easy to spot and avoid. The trickier problem is someone who pretends to be your friend while secretly trying to get you in trouble, so that is the person to be careful about.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two kinds of foe against each other: vaal-pola pakaivar (வாள்போல பகைவர், foes like a sword), whose hostility is open and therefore manageable, and kel-pol pakaivar (கேள்போல் பகைவர், foes who appear as kel, 'kin' or intimates). The imperative pair anjarka / anjuka (அஞ்சற்க / அஞ்சுக, 'fear not' / 'fear') gives the verse its antithetical snap. What is to be feared is their thodarpu (தொடர்பு), the ongoing association, since closeness is the very channel through which the hidden enemy works. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second group as those who behave like relatives while harbouring utpakai, and Pope renders them 'foes who seem like kinsmen'. The text agrees in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Duryodhana, outwardly welcoming his Pandava cousins, has a mansion of lac built at Varanavata for them, planning to burn them inside it.
hinduism.explanation: The plot hides lethal enmity behind the forms of family hospitality; the Pandavas escape only through Vidura's warning.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's 'enemy who appears as kin', more dangerous than any open swordsman.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha sub-parva (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match: an enemy disguised as a welcoming relative.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him; When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that the hater often hides behind gracious speech.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts tell us to fear the pleasant-faced foe more than the open one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-direct parallel on the danger of the concealed, friendly-seeming enemy.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he whose speech pleases you in worldly life, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the person whose agreeable words mask the most bitter hostility.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks the smooth-tongued hidden opponent as the most dangerous.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; the Qur'an speaks of hypocrisy generally rather than kinship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it ... But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says he could have endured or hidden from an open enemy, but betrayal by a close companion is unbearable.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's contrast exactly: the open foe is bearable, the intimate foe is the one to fear.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close structural match (open enemy vs. intimate); quoted with an ellipsis from the KJV.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha teaches young Sigala to recognize four kinds of foes who come in the guise of friends: the taker, the flatterer, the one who only talks, and the companion in ruin.
buddhism.explanation: The discourse gives practical signs for detecting enemies who present themselves as friends.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's warning to fear foes who wear the face of a friend or relative.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct thematic counterpart: foes disguised as friends.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demodocus sings of the wooden horse: the Trojans, deceived, drag the gift into their own city, and the Greeks hidden inside sack Troy from within.
greek_mythology.explanation: A city that withstood ten years of open siege falls to an enemy it welcomed inside its walls.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The open army was survivable; the enemy taken in as a friend proved fatal, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of a disguised enemy within, though the horse is a stratagem, not a false kinsman.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There are no intrigues more difficult to guard against than those which are concealed under a pretence of duty, or under the name of some intimate connection. For you can easily avoid one who is openly an adversary, by guarding against him; but this secret, internal, and domestic evil not only exists, but even overwhelms you before you can foresee it or examine into it.”
philosophy.explanation: Accusing Verres of betraying the consul he served as quaestor, Cicero argues that the treachery of a trusted associate is far more dangerous than open hostility.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero makes the Kural's own contrast: an open enemy can be guarded against, while an enemy in the guise of a friend or kinsman strikes before he is detected.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Against Verres (In Verrem), II.1.39 (tr. C. D. Yonge)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseids/Perseus (Yonge, The Orations of Marcus Tullius Cicero, vol. 1, 1903). Near one-to-one match of the open-enemy versus hidden-enemy contrast; the source is a forensic speech rather than a philosophical treatise.

kurals.tamil:
உட்பகை அஞ்சித்தற் காக்க உலைவிடத்து
மட்பகையின் மாணத் தெறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Utpakai anjiththar kaakka ulaivitaththu
matpakaiyin maanath therum.
kurals.meaning: Fear the enemy within and guard yourself, for in a moment of weakness it will cut you down as surely as the potter's tool cuts through clay.
kurals.elementary: A potter uses a thin wire or blade to slice through soft clay in one easy stroke. Hidden enemies wait for a time when you are tired or in trouble, and then they can hurt you just as easily, so it is wise to watch out for them early.
kurals.university: The verse pairs a command, utpakai anji thar kaakka (உட்பகை அஞ்சித் தற்காக்க, 'fearing internal enmity, guard yourself'), with a warning about timing: ulaividaththu (உலைவிடத்து), 'at the time of tottering' or decline. The image matpakai (மட்பகை), literally 'clay-enemy', is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the potter's cutting tool that slices clay vessels, so that maana therum (மாணத் தெறும்) means 'will destroy thoroughly'. Pope's 'potter's knife' follows the same reading. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads the second line as setting a cooking pot on an unfired clay vessel, an interpretive variant rather than a textual one. The Tamil text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Protect thyself, O king, from all fears that arise from within. Fears, however, that arise from outside are of little consequence. The first kind of fear, O king, may cut thy roots in a single day.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that internal dissension is the real danger to a ruler, able to destroy him suddenly.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural almost point for point: guard against the enemy within, which strikes all at once.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section CVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, verified against the Ganguli translation.

christianity.quote_or_event: In Gethsemane, while Jesus' disciples sleep, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrives with an armed crowd and betrays him with a kiss.
christianity.explanation: The betrayal comes from inside the inner circle and at the hour of greatest vulnerability.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural warns, the internal enemy strikes when one is weakest.
christianity._accuracy_note: Narrative match on timing and inner betrayal; the Gospels do not frame it as advice to guard oneself.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are the enemy, so beware of them.”
islam.explanation: Describing the hypocrites inside the Medinan community, whose appearance and speech are pleasing, the Qur'an names them the real enemy.
islam.tie_back: Both texts urge vigilance against the foe who lives within one's own community.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear match on 'beware the enemy within'; lacks the Kural's point about timing.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ahithophel, David's trusted counsellor, joins Absalom's rebellion; David prays that his counsel be turned to foolishness, and Ahithophel urges an immediate strike while David is weary and weak-handed.
judaism.explanation: The trusted insider knows exactly when the king is most vulnerable.
judaism.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural's warning that an internal enemy strikes in a time of weakness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel, including the timing of the attack.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that the most damaging enemy is the one inside oneself.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of a hostile insider, the Dhammapada of a hostile mind, but both rank the inner foe above the outer one.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the inner-vs-outer structure but moves the enemy from a person to the mind.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld, Agamemnon's shade tells Odysseus how he survived the Trojan War only to be killed at his own homecoming feast by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The victor of a ten-year war dies in his own house, at the moment he lets down his guard.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The enemy within strikes when defences are down, just as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of an enemy within striking at a vulnerable moment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his 1838 Lyceum Address, Abraham Lincoln argued that danger to the American republic would not come from abroad but would spring up from among its own people.
philosophy.explanation: Lincoln held that no external power could crush the nation, and that only internal disorder could destroy it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he identifies the internal enemy as the one to fear and guard against.
philosophy.source: Abraham Lincoln, Address before the Young Men's Lyceum of Springfield (1838)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; political rhetoric rather than formal philosophy, but a close thematic match.

kurals.tamil:
மனமாணா உட்பகை தோன்றின் இனமாணா
ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Manamaanaa utpakai thondrin inamaanaa
edham palavum tharum.
kurals.meaning: If hidden enmity arises in a mind that will not be reformed, it brings many troubles that turn one's own people against one.
kurals.elementary: If a person keeps a secret grudge and refuses to let it go, it slowly spoils everything around them. Soon brothers, sisters and friends are arguing and taking sides, and the whole group stops getting along.
kurals.university: The verse balances two negated compounds: mana-maanaa (மனமாணா, 'mind not made excellent', i.e. unreformed or unreconciled) and ina-maanaa (இனமாணா, 'kin not made excellent', i.e. kinsfolk who fall out of harmony). When utpakai arises in the first, it yields edham palavum (ஏதம் பலவும், many faults or evils) of the second kind. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the result as many faults that keep one's kin from being set right, while Kalaignar says such a disposition makes one's own people into enemies. Pope's 'secret enmities ... that minds pervert' and the thirukkural.net rendering 'myriad miseries manifest among kin' both preserve the link between inner hostility and outer estrangement. No textual variant is attested between ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his very mind will be the greatest enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that an unmastered mind becomes one's own worst enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural traces the troubles of utpakai back to an unreformed mind, just as the Gita locates the enemy in the uncontrolled mind.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the 'unreformed mind' element; the Gita does not address the social harm among kin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?”
christianity.explanation: James traces quarrels within the community back to disordered desires inside each person.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees outward discord among one's own people as the fruit of inner hostility.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on inner disorder producing communal strife.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet Muhammad told believers not to hate one another, envy one another or turn their backs on one another, but to be servants of God as brothers.
islam.explanation: The hadith treats hidden hatred and envy as the forces that break a community apart.
islam.tie_back: Both texts warn that concealed rancour destroys the bonds among one's own people.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; good thematic match on inner hatred dividing brothers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids nursing silent hatred and requires open, honest correction instead.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's 'unreformed' hidden enmity is exactly the hatred in the heart that Leviticus forbids.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on hidden hatred among kin; Leviticus prescribes the remedy rather than describing the damage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who harbor such thoughts do not still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada observes that nursing grievances keeps hatred alive.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the 'unreformed mind' of the Kural, from which hidden enmity and its many troubles keep arising.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the inner cause; does not address division among kin.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod lists the children of Eris (Strife): Toil, Forgetfulness, Famine, Sorrows, Fightings, Battles, Murders, Quarrels, Lies, Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth a single strife gives birth to a whole brood of evils.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that one hidden enmity yields 'many evils'.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on 'one strife, many evils'; Hesiod's Eris is cosmic, not specifically internal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself each morning that he will meet difficult people, but that all are made for cooperation, like hands, feet and eyelids, so that acting against one another is contrary to nature.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic emperor treats resentment toward one's fellows as a self-inflicted distortion of the mind.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he links an unreformed, resentful mind to the breakdown of a community meant to work as one body.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Moderate match; the Stoic focus is on self-discipline rather than the damage of hidden enmity.

kurals.tamil:
உறல்முறையான் உட்பகை தோன்றின் இறல்முறையான்
ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uralmuraiyaan utpakai thondrin iralmuraiyaan
edham palavum tharum.
kurals.meaning: If hidden enmity arises among those bound by kinship, it brings many deadly evils.
kurals.elementary: When a family has a big fight that nobody fixes, it can grow worse and worse until it breaks the family apart. The poet says a quarrel inside the family can be the most dangerous kind of all.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a chiming pair: ural-muraiyaan (உறல்முறையான், 'by way of relationship') and iral-muraiyaan (இறல்முறையான், 'by way of death'). Where enmity springs from kinship, it yields evils of a deadly kind. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as 'many sufferings of the kind that kill', and Solomon Pappaiah as 'many faults joined with death'. Pope's explanation speaks of internal hatred 'in a (king's) family' leading to 'fatal crime', showing the royal framing of the traditional commentary, where kin-enmity means dynastic feud. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads iral-muraiyaan differently, as harm extending even to those outside the kin, an interpretive variant. The Tamil text agrees in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On the field of Kurukshetra, Arjuna sees grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons and friends arrayed on both sides and despairs that the destruction of the family will ruin its ancient traditions.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata war is the great Indian epic of kin-enmity ending in near-total destruction.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's warning writ large: enmity within a family brings deadly ruin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong thematic fit; paraphrased from Arjuna's lament in chapter 1.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And a man’s foes shall be they of his own household.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus, echoing Micah 7:6, warns that the deepest divisions may run through one's own home.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts recognize that hostility within the family is especially grave.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on enmity within the household; Jesus speaks of division over faith, not of its deadly results.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an tells of the two sons of Adam: one's offering is accepted, the other's is not, and the jealous brother kills his brother, becoming one of the regretful.
islam.explanation: The first murder in the Qur'anic story arises from rivalry between brothers.
islam.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural's teaching that enmity among kin leads to deadly harm.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match on fatal kin-enmity; paraphrased.

judaism.quote_or_event: Cain, resentful that his brother Abel's offering is accepted and his is not, rises up against Abel in the field and kills him.
judaism.explanation: In Genesis the first killing in human history is fratricide born of jealousy.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's 'enmity by relationship' that brings 'evils by death' is embodied in Cain and Abel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Ajatasattu of Magadha, the son of King Bimbisara, had his own father killed to seize the throne, and later confessed this wrong before the Buddha.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts remember the patricide as a grave evil born of ambition within the royal family.
buddhism.tie_back: It exemplifies the Kural's warning about deadly enmity inside a dynasty.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel; the sutta records the confession, with the fuller story in the commentaries.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eteocles and Polynices, the sons of Oedipus, quarrel over the throne of Thebes; Polynices leads seven champions against the city, and the brothers kill each other at the seventh gate.
greek_mythology.explanation: The feud between brothers ends in mutual destruction, fulfilling their father's curse.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'enmity within kinship bringing deadly evils' in its starkest form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very strong match on fatal kin-enmity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Describing the civil strife at Corcyra, Thucydides observes that kinship became a weaker tie than party, and that fathers killed their sons in the violence.
philosophy.explanation: Thucydides analyses stasis, internal faction, as a force that dissolves even family bonds and unleashes every kind of death.
philosophy.tie_back: He confirms the Kural's insight that enmity within one's own people brings deadly evils.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 3.81-82
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on internal strife; paraphrased from the Corcyra narrative.

kurals.tamil:
ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Ondraamai ondriyaar katpatin egngnaandrum
pondraamai ondral aridhu.
kurals.meaning: Once discord takes hold among those who were united, it is ever hard to escape destruction.
kurals.elementary: Think of a team that always played together well. If the players start secretly disliking each other, they stop passing the ball and stop helping, and soon even an easy match is lost. Once a group splits, it is very hard to stop it from falling apart.
kurals.university: The couplet is a study in the root ondru (ஒன்று, 'to be one, to unite'): ondraamai (ஒன்றாமை, disunity) arises among ondriyaar (ஒன்றியார், those who were united), and then pondraamai ondral (பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல், 'attaining non-perishing', i.e. escaping ruin) becomes aridhu (அரிது, difficult) egngnaandrum (எஞ்ஞான்றும், at any time). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: when enmity arises among one's own people, it is always hard to avoid perishing through that internal enmity; Solomon Pappaiah applies it to a government whose fall cannot then be prevented. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as the difficulty of ever reuniting once a group is split by another's intrigue. Both sources print the same text, and thirukkural.net transliterates katpatin, reflecting the sandhi of kan + padin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra's first book, 'The Separation of Friends', the jackal Damanaka sows mistrust between the lion king Pingalaka and his close friend, the bull Sanjivaka, until the lion kills the bull.
hinduism.explanation: The frame story shows how a strong alliance is destroyed once suspicion is planted between its members.
hinduism.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural's teaching that discord among the united makes ruin almost inescapable.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match on broken union leading to destruction; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus states it as a general law: a divided kingdom, city or household cannot survive.
christianity.tie_back: This is nearly a restatement of the Kural's claim that disunity among the united leads to ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands the community to stay united and reminds it that it was once divided by enmity.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat unity as survival and division as the road to ruin.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on unity versus division; framed as a command rather than an observation.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the Second Temple fell, though its generation studied Torah and did good deeds, because of sinat chinam, baseless hatred among Jews, which it weighs as equal to idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed combined.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition locates the cause of national catastrophe in internal enmity rather than in the Roman army.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's lesson: once the united fall into enmity, destruction follows.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjians, the Buddha says they will prosper as long as they meet often and meet, act and disperse in harmony; tradition holds that they were later conquered only after their unity was broken by a planted agent.
buddhism.explanation: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta makes concord the first condition of a people's survival.
buddhism.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural: the united are safe until discord enters, after which ruin is hard to avoid.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match; the account of the Vajjians' later defeat comes from the commentarial tradition.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the close of the Eumenides, Athena prays that civil strife, insatiable of evil, may never roar in Athens and that citizens may not drink one another's blood in vengeance.
greek_mythology.explanation: The trilogy ends by naming civil discord as the gravest threat to the newly founded city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees internal division as the deadliest danger to a united people.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; good thematic match on civil strife.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks whether there is any greater evil for a city than what tears it apart and makes it many instead of one, or any greater good than what binds it together and makes it one.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats the unity of the city as its highest good and division as its worst evil.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly sees disunity among those once united as the gravest danger.

kurals.tamil:
செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே
உட்பகை உற்ற குடி.
kurals.transliteration:
Seppin punarchchipol kootinum kootaadhe
utpakai utra kuti.
kurals.meaning: A family gripped by hidden enmity may look joined like a casket and its lid, yet it is never truly united.
kurals.elementary: A box and its lid fit together neatly, but they are still two separate pieces that can be pulled apart at any moment. A family that is secretly angry inside may look together at dinner, but deep down they are not really united.
kurals.university: The governing image is seppin punarchchi (செப்பின் புணர்ச்சி, 'the joining of a seppu'), a small casket whose lid sits flush on its body so that the two look like one object. A kudi (குடி, family, clan or community) that has suffered utpakai may koodinum (கூடினும், even though it comes together) yet kootaadhu (கூடாதே, will surely not unite). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read seppu as a lidded casket, and Pope translates 'casket with its cover'. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads seppu as copper used to join two different metals, an interpretive variant. Pappaiah extends kudi to the party and the state. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The asura brothers Sunda and Upasunda, inseparable in everything and sharing one kingdom, fall into rivalry over the celestial maiden Tilottama and kill each other.
hinduism.explanation: Their seeming oneness hid a fault line that a single provocation split open.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the casket and lid, their union looked complete but did not hold once rivalry entered.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sunda-Upasunda episode, trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: The brothers were genuinely united before the rivalry, so this matches the fragility of union more than concealed enmity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares warm words over a hostile heart to cheap clay given a shiny coating.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts use a crafted-object image for outward togetherness covering inner hostility.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good image-level parallel; Proverbs describes an individual, not a family.

islam.quote_or_event: “Their violence among themselves is severe. You think they are together, but their hearts are diverse.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes a group that looks united from outside but is divided within.
islam.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's casket-and-lid image of apparent but unreal union.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on apparent unity hiding inner division.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph's brothers live under one roof as one family while hatred divides them.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's family, they are together in form but not in heart.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on a family outwardly together but inwardly divided; the hatred here is open rather than concealed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: At Kosambi, monks of a single community fell into a bitter dispute; they went on living in one monastery but refused to reconcile even when the Buddha himself urged them, and he finally withdrew to the forest alone.
buddhism.explanation: The community remained outwardly one Sangha while being split within.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's picture of a group joined in form but not in spirit.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 128, Upakkilesa Sutta (opening); Vinaya, Mahavagga X

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Atreus, pretending to be reconciled with his brother Thyestes, invites him to a feast of welcome and secretly serves him the flesh of his own sons.
greek_mythology.explanation: A show of family reunion conceals the most savage enmity in Greek myth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's casket and lid in tragic form: apparent union, total inner hostility.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on feigned reconciliation hiding enmity; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that friendships based on utility or pleasure dissolve easily once the advantage ends, because the partners never loved each other for who they were.
philosophy.explanation: Such friendships look like friendship but lack its inner substance.
philosophy.tie_back: This loosely matches the Kural's union that looks complete but is not real.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best match: Aristotle speaks of shallow friendship, not concealed enmity.

kurals.tamil:
அரம்பொருத பொன்போலத் தேயும் உரம்பொருது
உட்பகை உற்ற குடி.
kurals.transliteration:
Aramporudha ponpolath theyum uramporudhu
utpakai utra kuti.
kurals.meaning: A family afflicted by internal enmity wears itself down, its strength rubbed away, like metal worn by a file.
kurals.elementary: When you rub a file back and forth on a piece of metal, a little dust falls off each time until the metal gets thinner and thinner. A family that keeps fighting inside loses a little strength every day in the same way, until there is not much left.
kurals.university: The image is aram porudha pon (அரம் பொருத பொன், metal struck by a file), which theyum (தேயும், wears away). The second line, uram porudhu (உரம் பொருது), means that the family's own strength (uram) is ground away by the friction of utpakai. Pon usually means gold, as Pope and thirukkural.net render it, but Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as iron (இரும்பு), reflecting the wider sense of pon as metal. The echo of porudha / porudhu (struck / striking) emphasises that the family is both the file and the metal, wearing itself down. The text agrees in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Samba, cursed by sages his kinsmen had mocked, produces an iron bolt, King Ugrasena has it ground into fine powder and cast into the sea; the Vrishnis and Andhakas later destroy one another, and the Mahabharata says they were consumed by that iron bolt.
hinduism.explanation: The Yadava clan, invincible to outsiders, perishes in a drunken quarrel among its own members.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the clan's strength is ground away from within, and the epic even uses the image of iron filed to powder.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 1 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on self-destruction of a clan, with a striking filed-iron image; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns the Galatian church that infighting will wear the community away.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts picture internal friction slowly consuming a group's strength.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on mutual attrition from within.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that internal disputes sap a community's courage and strength.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says quarrelling within makes a group's strength wear away.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on internal strife draining strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: After Solomon's death, the people quarrel with his son Rehoboam, and the ten northern tribes break away, leaving Israel split into two rival kingdoms.
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew Bible presents the division as a lasting weakening of the nation.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's image of strength worn down by internal friction fits the divided kingdom.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit; the split is sudden rather than a gradual wearing-down.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After the death of the Jain leader Nigantha Nataputta, his followers split into factions and attacked one another with sharp words; the Buddha then taught Ananda ways of settling disputes so that his own Sangha would not suffer the same fate.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses a neighbouring community's decay through infighting as a warning.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's picture of a group wearing itself away through internal enmity is exactly what the sutta describes.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles over a captive woman leads Achilles to withdraw from battle, and the Greek army suffers heavy losses at Trojan hands.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad opens with internal discord that weakens the Greeks more than any enemy has.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's filed metal, the army loses its strength through friction within its own ranks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nam concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia maximae dilabuntur.”
philosophy.explanation: The dying King Micipsa tells his sons that through harmony small states grow, while through discord the greatest fall apart.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's principle in Latin: internal discord wears down even the greatest strength.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Latin verified; the translation in the explanation is a free rendering.

kurals.tamil:
எட்பக வன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்
உட்பகை உள்ளதாங் கேடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Etpaka vanna sirumaiththe aayinum
utpakai ulladhaang ketu.
kurals.meaning: Even if internal enmity is as small as a split sesame seed, ruin lies within it.
kurals.elementary: A sesame seed is one of the tiniest seeds there is, and half a seed is smaller still. The poet says even a grudge that small, kept hidden inside a group, can grow until it breaks everything apart.
kurals.university: The measure of smallness is etpakavu (எட்பகவு, the split half of a sesame seed), among the tiniest units in Tamil idiom; anna (அன்ன) means 'like'. However sirumaiththu (சிறுமைத்து, slight) the utpakai is, ketu (கேடு, ruin) is ulladhu (உள்ளது, present) within it. Mu. Varadarasanar says that even at that size it carries ruin able to destroy a whole family, and Solomon Pappaiah reads it as destruction already present inside the faction. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads 'ulladhu' as 'all that exists', giving 'ruin to everything', a reading the word order allows. The thirukkural.net rendering ('even a dissent as small as a seed') and Pope ('slight as shred of sesame seed') agree with the dominant reading. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Maya Sabha, Duryodhana mistakes a crystal floor for water and falls into a pool he took for solid floor, and Bhima and others laugh at him; the humiliation feeds the envy behind the dice game and the war.
hinduism.explanation: A small moment of mockery within the extended family helps set off the Kurukshetra catastrophe.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural warns, a slight internal grievance can hold ruin within it.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Duryodhana's account of the palace)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Popular retellings attribute the laughter to Draupadi, which is a later elaboration; the epic's causes of the war are also many.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a tiny spark, like a careless word, can set a whole forest ablaze.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts insist that a small seed of discord carries vast destructive power.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on small causes of great ruin; James focuses on speech.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that Satan has despaired of being worshipped by the believers in Arabia, but has not given up on sowing dissension among them.
islam.explanation: The hadith presents internal discord as the opening through which harm still enters a community.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats even small internal division as dangerous.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; matches the danger of internal dissension but not the specific point about its smallness.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud says Jerusalem was destroyed because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza: a host's servant invited the wrong man to a feast, the host publicly threw out his enemy, the sages present stayed silent, and the humiliated guest went to Rome and informed against the Jews.
judaism.explanation: A trivial mix-up between two similar names, combined with an existing grudge, sets off national catastrophe.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's sesame-seed enmity: tiny in origin, ruinous in effect.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Think not lightly of evil, saying, ‘It will not come to me.’ Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that small wrongs, ignored, accumulate into great harm.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly refuses to treat small enmity as harmless.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the theme of small things becoming great; refers to personal evil, not internal enmity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eris, the goddess of Strife, throws a golden apple inscribed for the fairest among the goddesses at a wedding feast; the quarrel between Hera, Athena and Aphrodite leads to the judgement of Paris and the Trojan War.
greek_mythology.explanation: A single apple becomes the seed of the most famous war in Greek myth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, strife no bigger than a seed can hold enormous ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image match on a tiny seed of strife; the quarrel is among goddesses, not within a human family.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In revolutions the occasions may be trifling, but great interests are at stake. Even trifles are most important when they concern the rulers.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle cites how the constitution of Syracuse was overturned by a love-quarrel between two young men in the government.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he warns that the smallest internal dispute among those in power can bring down the state.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match, verified against the Jowett translation.

kurals.tamil:
உடம்பாடு இலாதவர் வாழ்க்கை குடங்கருள்
பாம்போடு உடனுறைந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Utampaatu ilaadhavar vaazhkkai kutangarul
paampotu utanurain thatru.
kurals.meaning: Living together with those who are not truly in agreement with you is like sharing a small hut with a snake.
kurals.elementary: Imagine sleeping in a tiny tent with a snake curled up in the corner. You could never relax, because you would always be wondering when it might bite. Living with someone who secretly dislikes you feels the same way.
kurals.university: The closing couplet gives the chapter its most vivid image. Utampaatu ilaadhavar (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) are 'those without inner agreement', people who share one's life without sharing one's mind. To live with them is kutangarul paampotu utanurainthatru (குடங்கருள் பாம்போடு உடனுறைந்தற்று), 'like dwelling together with a snake inside a kutangar'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss kutangar as a small hut (குடிசை), and Kalaignar stresses the moment-by-moment fear of such a life. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as a dark cave, an interpretive variant. Pope's 'dwelling in a shed with snake for company' and thirukkural.net's 'share a hut with a cobra' agree on the hut reading. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “internal troubles like the fear from a lurking snake are more serious than external troubles.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya advises a king to deal with internal danger first, comparing it to a snake hidden close by.
hinduism.tie_back: The Arthashastra and the Kural use the same image: an internal enemy is a snake inside one's own dwelling.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book IX (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Remarkably close image and teaching, verified against the Shamasastry translation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?”
christianity.explanation: The prophet Amos asks a rhetorical question: true companionship requires real agreement.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts hold that a shared life without inner accord cannot be safe or real.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on the need for agreement; lacks the Kural's image of danger.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that a believer is not stung twice from the same hole.
islam.explanation: The hadith uses the image of a snake or scorpion hole to teach vigilance against a known source of harm.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's snake imagery and its counsel to stay alert to danger close at hand.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the image and the call to vigilance but does not address living with hostile companions; a next-best match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs values a peaceful home with little over a rich home full of conflict.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts hold that sharing a home without harmony makes life unbearable.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on the misery of a discordant household; lacks the hidden-danger image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a seeker not find a companion who is better or equal, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with the fool.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada advises going alone rather than living with an unsuitable companion.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats companionship without real accord as worse than solitude.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on avoiding companions without accord; concerns fools rather than hidden enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable, a farmer finds a snake frozen with cold, warms it in his bosom, and is bitten to death once it revives.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable warns that taking a hostile nature into one's closest space invites a deadly bite.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's snake in the hut: closeness with a hostile companion is mortal danger.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, The Farmer and the Snake (Perry 176)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image match; Aesop is Greek fable rather than mythology.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca advises Lucilius to avoid crowds and keep company with those who will make him better, because close association with others' vices does harm.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic letter treats one's companions as a decisive influence on peace of mind and character.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that sharing life with the wrong people costs one's safety and peace.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best match: Seneca speaks of moral contagion, not hidden enmity.
